content: Sweetness is one of the five fundamental tastes and is almost universally perceived as a pleasurable sensation. Foods high in simple carbohydrates, such as sugar, are most commonly associated with sweetness. However, there are other natural and artificial compounds that are significantly sweeter, some of which are used as sugar substitutes for individuals with a preference for sweet flavors. Certain compounds can also modify the perception of sweetness itself. The chemosensory mechanism for detecting sweetness, which varies among individuals and species, has only been elucidated in recent years. The current theoretical framework is the multipoint attachment theory, which posits that multiple binding sites exist between the sweetness receptor and the sweet substance. Examples of Sweet Substances A wide variety of chemical compounds, including aldehydes and ketones, exhibit sweetness. Among biological substances, all simple carbohydrates are sweet to some degree. Sucrose, commonly known as sugar, is the prototypical example of a sweet substance, although fructose is slightly sweeter. Some amino acids, such as alanine, glycine, and serine, are mildly sweet, while others may be perceived as both sweet and bitter. Certain plant species produce glycosides that are significantly sweeter than sugar. For instance, glycyrrhizin, the sweet component of licorice root, is approximately 30 times sweeter than sucrose. Another example is stevioside, derived from the South American shrub Stevia rebaudiana, which is about 250 times sweeter than sucrose. Additionally, sweet proteins like thaumatin, found in the West African katemfe fruit, and hen egg lysozyme, an antibiotic protein in chicken eggs, are also sweet. Even some inorganic compounds, such as beryllium chloride and lead acetate, are sweet. The latter may have contributed to lead poisoning among the ancient Roman aristocracy, as the Roman delicacy sapa was prepared by boiling soured wine in lead pots. Hundreds of synthetic organic compounds are known to be sweet, but only a small number are legally approved as food additives. For example, while chloroform, nitrobenzene, and ethylene glycol are sweet, they are also toxic. As of 2005, seven artificial sweeteners are widely used: saccharin, cyclamate, aspartame, acesulfame potassium, sucralose, alitame, and neotame. Cyclamate was temporarily banned in the U.S., and saccharin faced a similar situation in Canada. Sweetness Modifiers Certain substances can alter the perception of sweetness. One class of these compounds inhibits the perception of sweet tastes, whether from sugars or potent sweeteners. Lactisole, a compound produced by Domino Sugar, is commercially significant and is used in some jellies and fruit preserves to enhance fruit flavors by suppressing excessive sweetness. Two natural products, gymnemic acid (from the leaves of the Indian vine Gymnema sylvestre) and ziziphin (from the leaves of the Chinese jujube Ziziphus jujuba), also exhibit sweetness-inhibiting properties. Gymnemic acid has been widely promoted in herbal medicine as a treatment for sugar cravings and diabetes mellitus. Conversely, two plant proteins, miraculin and curculin, cause sour foods to taste sweet. After exposure to these proteins, sourness is perceived as sweetness for up to an hour. While curculin has some inherent sweetness, miraculin is tasteless on its own. The Sweetness Receptor Despite the wide variety of chemical substances known to be sweet and the understanding that the ability to perceive sweetness resides in taste buds on the tongue, the biomolecular mechanism of sweetness was elusive until relatively recently. As late as the 1990s, there was uncertainty about whether a single sweetness receptor existed. A breakthrough occurred in 2001 when experiments with laboratory mice revealed that mice with different versions of the gene T1R3 exhibited varying preferences for sweet foods. Subsequent research demonstrated that the T1R3 protein forms a complex with a related protein, T1R2, to create a G-protein-coupled receptor that serves as the sweetness receptor in mammals. Sweetness perception varies significantly between species. For example, New World monkeys do not find aspartame sweet, whereas Old World monkeys, apes, and humans do. Members of the family Felidae, such as cats, are unable to perceive sweetness at all. Historical Theories of Sweetness The development of organic chemistry in the 19th century introduced numerous new chemical compounds and methods for determining their molecular structures. Early organic chemists often tasted their products, either intentionally for characterization or accidentally due to poor laboratory hygiene. In 1914, German chemist Georg Cohn proposed that molecules must contain specific structural motifs, called sapophores, to evoke a particular taste. Regarding sweetness, he noted that molecules with multiple hydroxyl groups or chlorine atoms were often sweet and that smaller molecules within a series of structurally similar compounds tended to be sweeter than larger ones. In 1919, Oertly and Myers proposed a more elaborate theory based on the then-current understanding of color in synthetic dyes. They hypothesized that sweet compounds must contain two structural motifs: a glucophore and an auxogluc. They identified six candidate glucophores and nine auxoglucs based on known sweet compounds. The theory of sweetness received little further academic attention until 1963, when Robert Shallenberger and Terry Acree proposed the AH-B theory of sweetness. According to this theory, the AH-B unit of a sweetener binds to a corresponding AH-B unit on the biological sweetness receptor to produce the sensation of sweetness. A later refinement, the AH-B-X theory proposed by Lemont Kier in 1972, suggested that sweet compounds must have a third binding site (labeled X) that interacts with a hydrophobic site on the sweetness receptor via London dispersion forces. The most elaborate theory of sweetness to date is the multipoint attachment (MPA) theory proposed by Jean-Marie Tinti and Claude Nofre in 1991. This theory involves a total of eight interaction sites between a sweetener and the sweetness receptor, although not all sweeteners interact with all eight sites. This model has successfully guided efforts to discover highly potent sweeteners, including the most potent family of sweeteners known to date, the guanidine sweeteners. The most potent of these, lugduname, is approximately 225,000 times sweeter than sucrose.
